opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's early but very real. Once a company has more than a handful of engineers using coding agents seriously, the questions shift from "does this work?" to "how do we manage it?" Which agents are people using, what are they spending, which tasks succeed and which get thrown away, and is any of this actually making us ship faster or just producing more code to review?

There's a lot of similarity to what happened with data and ML. First everyone experiments, then you need observability, governance, and cost control, because the thing has become core infrastructure. With agents it's sharper because they act. They touch your codebase, run commands, and sometimes reach production systems. So you need traces of what the agent did and why, permissions, and audit logs, not just a dashboard of token counts.

I'd split the market into a few layers. One is observability and evaluation: understanding agent sessions, measuring quality, catching regressions when you change models or prompts. Another is governance and security: which repos and tools an agent can touch, what data it can see, and policy enforcement. A third is economics: attribution of cost and value, because these bills can get big fast and finance teams will start asking. And the most interesting one long-term is a feedback loop, where you take all those traces and use them to make agents better on your specific codebase, almost like a learning system for your org.

The open question is who owns it. The agent vendors will build some of this, but enterprises usually don't want to be locked into one agent, and most teams already use several. So I think there's room for a neutral layer that works across agents, similar to how data platforms sit across many tools. And it'll probably merge with the existing developer productivity and data platforms rather than stay a standalone category forever. But right now it's a pretty open field, and the companies that figure out how to measure real outcomes, not just activity, will have a big advantage.

r001.rationale: The response discusses management software layers and market development, but does not predict that consultants will serve the market before dedicated management-plane software.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's going to be a big market, and honestly I think it's going to look a lot like what happened with data pipelines and ML over the past decade, just compressed into a much shorter time frame.

The way I think about it is: right now most teams are in the phase where they're just excited the agents work at all. Someone sets up Claude Code or Cursor or whatever, they get a PR out of it, everyone's thrilled. But the moment you go from one engineer experimenting to a few hundred engineers and a bunch of agents running in CI, the questions change completely. It's no longer "can it write code?" It's "which of these agents are actually producing changes we merge? Where are they burning tokens and not producing value? What fraction of their PRs get reverted a week later? Which repos or which types of tasks are they good at, and which ones should we not even point them at?"

And nobody has good answers to that today. If you ask most engineering leaders what their agents cost per merged change, or what the defect rate is on agent-written code versus human-written code, they genuinely don't know. That's exactly the kind of gap where a management layer shows up.

I'd break it into a few pieces. One is observability, which is the obvious part: traces, tool calls, token usage, latency, how often the agent went off into the weeds. We saw this with LLM apps generally, where tracing turned out to be the thing everyone needed first, and the same thing is true for coding agents, maybe even more so because the trajectories are so long. An agent might take two hundred steps to fix a bug, and if you can't see those steps, you can't debug it or improve it.

The second piece is evaluation, and I think this is where it gets more interesting and more differentiated. Coding is actually one of the better domains for eval because you have ground truth: tests pass or they don't, the PR got merged or it didn't, the code got reverted or it stayed. So you can build pretty rigorous measurement here in a way that's harder for, say, a customer support agent. But it's not free. You need to collect those signals systematically, you need to tie them back to the specific agent configuration and prompt and model that produced them, and you need to do it at a scale where you can actually detect that version B is better than version A. That's a real system to build.

The third piece is the governance and control side, which I think people underrate. Once agents are committing code, you want policies: what repos can they touch, what secrets can they see, what has to get human review, what's the budget per team. Enterprises will not deploy these things broadly without that, and the agent vendors themselves are not really incentivized to build the neutral layer that works across all of them.

That last point is probably the most important structural thing. Most companies are going to use more than one agent. They'll have a couple of IDE agents, something running autonomously in CI, maybe internal ones built on the SDKs. So there's a natural need for a cross-vendor layer that sits above all of them, and historically that layer tends to be a separate product from the thing being managed. It's the same reason you have Datadog instead of just using every cloud's built-in monitoring.

Now, will that be a standalone company, or does it get absorbed into existing platforms? I think both. Some of it will show up in the dev platforms, GitHub, GitLab, whoever, because they already own the PR and the merge signal. Some of it shows up in the data and ML platforms, because at the end of the day this is a data problem: you're collecting traces and outcomes and running analytics and training things on top of them. And there'll be startups that go deep on it and build genuinely better tooling, and some of them will do very well.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking of it as "dashboards for agents." The interesting version is closed-loop. You collect all this telemetry not just to look at it but to feed it back: automatically figure out which tasks to route to which agent, automatically tune the instructions and context you're giving them, flag the patterns where they consistently fail and turn those into evals. The teams that do that are going to get a compounding advantage, because their agents get measurably better every month and everyone else's stay roughly the same.

So, short version: yes, big market, it's going to form faster than people expect, and the winners will be the ones who treat it as a measurement and optimization system rather than just monitoring.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a large market and discusses startups and platform products, but it does not say consultants will serve the market before dedicated management-plane software.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s going to be a pretty substantial market there, because once you have multiple coding agents working, you need some way to understand what they’re doing and whether they’re actually helping. How much are you spending? Which tasks are they succeeding at? How much time does a person spend reviewing or fixing the output? Just counting how much code they generate doesn’t really answer those questions.

The interesting question is how much of that becomes part of the agent products themselves versus a separate layer. I’d expect the agent vendors to provide basic monitoring and management. But if a company is using several different agents, there’s value in having a consistent way to evaluate them and decide which one to use for which task.

And I think evaluation and management become closely connected. If you can reliably tell whether a change meets your requirements, you can give the agent more autonomy. If you can’t, you end up having a human check every step. So the software that helps you establish that confidence could be quite valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agent vendors and a possible separate management layer, but does not say consultants will serve the market before dedicated management software.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s going to be a pretty interesting market there, because as you have more agents writing code, the bottleneck shifts to understanding what they’re doing and whether it’s actually useful. You can generate a lot of changes, but somebody has to decide: Did this solve the problem? Is the code maintainable? How much did it cost to get there?

So I’d expect tools for evaluating agents, tracking their work, and helping people review and manage it. The interesting question is how much of that gets built into the coding tools themselves versus becoming a separate layer. If a company is using multiple agents, there’s a good reason to want a common way to measure them and set policies. But I think the workflows are still evolving, so it’s early to know exactly where those boundaries will land.

r001.rationale: The response predicts tools for evaluating, tracking, reviewing, and managing coding agents, but it does not say consultants will serve the market before dedicated management software.
